summary: Juan Peredo opens by addressing the hype around AI-accelerated coding: tools like Codium and Cursor speed development but cannot fully build applications. Model choice depends on task complexity—simple tasks suit any LLM, while complex tasks may require stronger models like DeepSeek V3 or Claude. He contrasts traditional application architecture with AI-augmented applications, which add concerns around model selection, fine-tuning versus prompt engineering versus RAG, hallucination prevention, frequent model replacement, and GPU-based hosting. Hosting tools include Ollama for local exploration, Hugging Face Transformers for local inference, Modal for Python-based containerized cloud deployment, and SkyPilot for multi-cloud cost optimization. Building a chatbot is trivial, but validating output is hard—an LLM answered 3×3 as 33. Mitigation techniques include prompt engineering (imprecise, sometimes ignored), guardrails using a secondary classifier LLM (adds latency and cost), RAG (quality depends on vector database data relevance), and fine-tuning (expensive, slow, potentially degrading model quality). He stresses continuous evaluation using Ollama, Hugging Face Spaces, Open Router (routing prompts to cheapest provider), and LangSmith (recording runs and comparing model performance over time). He emphasizes externalizing prompts via repositories like LangChain Hub, enabling domain experts to collaboratively refine prompts without coding, and future-proofing against frequent model releases. Peredo then introduces agents—LLMs that break out of chatbot confines to interact with the real world by autonomously calling tools across multiple nodes. While powerful, agents introduce latency from multiple sequential LLM calls; parallel execution and branching via platforms like LangChain, LlamaIndex, and LangFlow can mitigate this. Cost is a major concern: a call center example with OpenAI o1 (3,000 calls/day, 15 tool calls each) costs $24/call, $9,270/day, ~$300,000/month. Replacing o1 with Llama 3.3 70b reduces this to $0.52/call and ~$50,000/month. He highlights over 20x price differences between models and significant output speed variations (Cerebras at 2,000+ tokens/sec versus 29-31 tokens/sec for slower providers). Finally, he addresses agent observability: debugging agents is far harder than deterministic applications because probabilistic models introduce unpredictable failures. He demonstrates LangSmith tracing, which shows the ordered sequence of LLM calls (e.g., Llama Guard, then Llama 3.1, then Mistral), along with metadata, inputs, outputs, and error tracking, enabling precise diagnosis of agent behavior.

sections.title: Introduction & AI Coding Reality Check
sections.summary: Juan Peredo introduces himself and addresses the hype around AI-accelerated coding. Tools like Codium and Cursor help, and LLMs can generate code, but they cannot fully build applications. Model choice depends on task complexity.

sections.title: AI-Added Application Complexity
sections.summary: Adding AI to applications introduces new concerns beyond traditional architecture: model selection, fine-tuning, prompt engineering, RAG, hallucination prevention, model replacement due to rapid releases, and GPU hosting decisions.

sections.title: Hosting Strategies & Tools
sections.summary: Discusses hosting options: Ollama and Hugging Face Transformers for local exploration, traditional cloud providers (Google Cloud, AWS, Azure), and simplified deployment tools Modal (Python decorators, containerized cloud deployment) and SkyPilot (multi-cloud cost optimization).

sections.title: Chatbot Validation Challenge
sections.summary: Building a chatbot is now easy with frameworks, but validating correctness is hard. Peredo shares an anecdote where an LLM answered 3×3 as 33, illustrating output reliability challenges.

sections.title: Output Quality Techniques
sections.summary: Covers mitigation techniques: prompt engineering (imprecise, sometimes ignored), guardrails with a secondary classifier LLM (adds latency and cost), RAG (quality depends on vector database data), and fine-tuning (expensive, slow, may degrade quality). No single technique guarantees correct output.

sections.title: Evaluation & Exploration Tools
sections.summary: Recommends continuous evaluation: Ollama for running hundreds of LLMs locally, Hugging Face Spaces for exploring open-source models and community code, and Open Router for routing prompts to the cheapest provider for a given model, with personal cost savings cited.

sections.title: LangSmith & Prompt Externalization
sections.summary: Introduces LangSmith by the LangChain creators for recording LLM runs and comparing model performance over time. Emphasizes externalizing prompts via repositories like LangChain Hub so domain experts can collaboratively refine prompts without coding, and future-proofing against frequent new model releases. Prompts should never be hardcoded in application code.

sections.title: Agents: LLMs Beyond Chatbots
sections.summary: Introduces agents as LLMs that break out of chatbot confines to interact with the real world by autonomously calling tools (functions) across multiple nodes. Examples include translating books and creating audio. The assistant node embeds an LLM that decides which tools to call and in what order, making autonomous decisions without hardcoded paths.

sections.title: Agent Latency & Cost Analysis
sections.summary: Agents introduce latency from multiple sequential LLM calls (e.g., 12-15 seconds). Parallel execution and branching via platforms like LangChain, LlamaIndex, and LangFlow reduce total time. A call center example with OpenAI o1 (3,000 calls/day, 15 tool calls each) costs $24/call, $9,270/day, ~$300,000/month. Costs scale linearly with each additional user.

sections.title: Model Selection: Price & Speed Tradeoffs
sections.summary: GPUs cost $4-5/hour versus CPUs at cents/hour. Over 20x price difference exists between cheapest and most expensive models. Output speed varies dramatically: Cerebras runs Llama 3.1 70b at 2,000+ tokens/sec while some providers run at 29-31 tokens/sec. Replacing OpenAI o1 with Llama 3.3 70b reduces call center cost from ~$300K/month to ~$50K/month. Smaller models are faster, cheaper, and better for the environment.

sections.title: Agent Observability & LangSmith Tracing
sections.summary: Debugging agents is far harder than deterministic applications because probabilistic models introduce unpredictable failures. Peredo shares a case where an agent failed because a user entered lowercase 'John' instead of capitalized; the fix was adding 'ignore case' to the externalized prompt. He demonstrates LangSmith tracing, which shows the ordered sequence of LLM calls (e.g., Llama Guard, then Llama 3.1, then Mistral) with metadata, inputs, outputs, and error tracking. He stresses that observability must be built or adopted—it is essential for diagnosing agent behavior across multiple nodes and LLM calls.
